name: Ivan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. Walk me through a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Ivan Gupta, 58, and still a junior lineworker after getting my vocational certificate two years ago. I used to maintain building lifts, so I know tools, but live power lines demand a different kind of patience. I check the truck’s test kit, set the work zone, and build or repair overhead lines under the crew leader’s supervision. I like tracing a fault back to one damaged connection. My hands are quick; my eye for the right clearance is still catching up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the truck like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leena works at a community clinic, and our grown son lives on his own. We have about five months of expenses put by, from years of careful spending, but I do not know what retirement income will be. I use AI every day to quiz myself on line diagrams and draft questions for the trainer; I check the answers with the manual because a wrong distance can hurt someone. I belong to the union and want training open to older new starters too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew that the AI fuss has settled and the real work is still in the field. Maybe the office gets its forms done sooner; I will still measure the clearance myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep learning the job if the work stays much the same. Leena’s clinic hours and our savings make the household fairly sound for now, but five months is not a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep using my evening AI quiz for line diagrams and ask the trainer to mark the answers I missed. In 2029 I’d take my regular line shifts and put thirty from each pay toward a larger cash reserve, because retirement is still a question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled with room to improve. The picture is ordinary enough that my biggest worry is making a mistake, not a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI quiz get something wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the quiz gave me the wrong clearance near a service drop. I caught it in the manual and wrote the correct number inside my helmet lid. A wrong distance can hurt someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you know about retirement money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a pension account from lift work, but I have not asked for a projection. I cannot count an amount I have not seen, even if Leena teases me for keeping every old payslip.

say: I’d tell coworkers **field repairs** still need measurements made at the actual pole.
I’d welcome **faster forms** without changing how we check a live line.
think: I expect to keep learning this job, with **clinic pay** and savings supporting us for now.
Our **five-month reserve** is useful but does not settle retirement.
do: Use the **AI line quiz** nightly and verify answers with the trainer.
Take regular **line shifts** in 2029 and put thirty per pay aside.
feel: I feel **settled and curious**, with safety mistakes more immediate than automation.
S0.quote: A wrong distance can hurt someone.
fieldNote: Ivan’s daily **AI quiz** is a study aid, never his authority for electrical clearances.
With five months saved and a second household income, he has **breathing room** despite being a junior worker.

steps.text: Use the AI line quiz and verify missed answers with the trainer
Take regular paid line shifts through 2029
Put thirty from each pay into a larger cash reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that dispatch software might spare us pointless drives, so I want to test it on real calls. I would also ask the union to check that a faster route does not become a shorter safety allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think paperwork and scheduling jobs will shrink before line repairs do. My own junior hours could become patchy if the company squeezes more calls into each truck, and Leena’s clinic may use AI for bookings without cutting care staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask to join a supervised trial of the dispatch app and record every route error we find. In 2029 I’d keep taking repairs, bring the error log to the union safety meeting, and practice using AI to compare the day’s work orders with the truck inventory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested, though there is a knot in my stomach about targets. A cleaner route would help us; a stopwatch attached to every pole would not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a map sent us to the rear gate of a substation with no truck access. I want that kind of mistake logged before a manager calls the app reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Leena see the same change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena has already seen automated booking suggestions at the clinic. She checks them against patients’ actual needs, and we would review both payslips if her hours changed.

say: I’d test **dispatch software** on real calls before praising it.
I’d ask our **union** to guard time for electrical checks.
think: I expect **office scheduling** to shrink before physical line repairs.
My **junior hours** could become patchy if crews get compressed into fewer trucks.
do: Join a **supervised dispatch trial** and log wrong routes.
Keep taking **repair shifts** in 2029 and bring errors to the union meeting.
Use **AI work orders** to cross-check truck inventory before departure.
feel: I feel **interested but tense** about faster targets on poles.
S1.quote: A cleaner route would help us; a stopwatch attached to every pole would not.
fieldNote: Ivan wants to test an app against real access problems, including a **blocked substation gate**.
His enthusiasm for tools is paired with a specific **union safety limit** on time pressure.

steps.text: Join a supervised dispatch trial and cross-check AI orders with truck inventory
Keep taking paid repair shifts through 2029
Bring the dispatch error log to the union safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI by 2028 could plan outages faster than our office, but a human crew still climbs until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for a public list of paid roles the company expects to keep during the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when thinking AI arrives and 63 when robots can take physical work. I may have five months saved, yet I could lose a junior line place before any retirement date I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d ask the training manager to show me the robot inspection pilot, if there is one, and enroll in a funded equipment-maintenance course if a place opens. In 2029 I’d keep paid line shifts and apply for the utility’s maintenance trainee post if advertised; I’d ask the union to insist on real vacancies before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, even though I want to see the machines up close. Curiosity cannot carry my partner Leena and me through a decade without my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old skill might transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can maintain motors from my lift years, but a line robot’s controls would be new to me. I would need an actual paid course, not a video link and a promise that everyone can adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena and I would stop replacing our car this year and use the reserve only if pay stopped. Our son pays his own rent, and I would rather not move the cost of my job loss to him.

say: I’d explain **2028 thinking AI** could plan outages before robots climb around 2031.
I’d ask for a **public list** of real paid positions during the transition.
think: At **63**, I could lose junior linework before retirement is affordable.
Our **five-month reserve** cannot replace my wage for years.
do: Visit a **robot inspection pilot** if one exists and seek funded maintenance training.
Keep **paid line shifts** in 2029 and apply for a maintenance trainee vacancy.
Ask the **union** for a list of actual openings before 2031.
feel: I feel **alarmed and curious**, aware that interest does not pay our bills.
S2.quote: Curiosity cannot carry my partner Leena and me through a decade without my wage.
fieldNote: Ivan looks for **equipment maintenance** because of his lift background, while admitting line robot controls would be new.
He keeps the five-month reserve intact and avoids shifting a **lost wage** onto his grown son.

steps.text: Enroll in a funded equipment-maintenance course if a place opens
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Apply for the utility maintenance trainee post if advertised
Ask the union to seek a list of real vacancies before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew five years should be enough to test equipment before betting jobs on it. Full thinking AI in 2031 would change outage plans and records; capable robots around 2034 would reach the climbing itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the first date and 66 at the robot date. I might want to retire then. Wanting retirement is different from having the pension numbers and enough money for my partner Leena and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a pension projection and ask the company whether maintainers are being trained for its equipment. I’d learn the new inspection software with the trainer; in 2032 I’d keep line shifts and apply for an equipment maintenance opening if one was posted, then review the projection with Leena before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel focused rather than trapped. Five years gives me room to test a new path, though I would not call a maintenance post safe after robots can maintain each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the maintenance idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a trained maintainer to show me one fault log before signing up for a course. A good match between my old motor work and the new gear would be evidence, not a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the pension estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the pension projection home and put it beside our rent, clinic pay and basic bills. If the numbers failed, we would keep seeking paid work instead of declaring an early retirement.

say: I’d ask for **real equipment tests** before the company changes line jobs.
I’d distinguish **2031 planning** from capable robots climbing around 2034.
think: I may need wages at **66** even if I want to retire.
Maintenance might also change after **capable robots** arrive, so I cannot treat it as permanent.
do: Request a **pension projection** and ask about equipment training.
Learn **inspection software** with the trainer and keep line shifts in 2032.
Apply for a **maintenance opening** if the company posts one.
feel: I feel **focused**, with time to test a path but no guaranteed refuge.
S3.quote: Wanting retirement is different from having the pension numbers and enough money for my partner Leena and me.
fieldNote: Ivan’s interest in maintenance is grounded in **old motor work** and a proposed test of an actual fault log.
He treats a pension projection as evidence to compare with **rent and bills**, not a promise of easy retirement.

steps.text: Request a pension projection and compare it with household bills
Learn inspection software with the company trainer
Keep taking paid line shifts in 2032
Apply for a posted equipment-maintenance opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my friends a ten-year warning gives us time to set up proper training and retirement choices. Thinking AI could run records in 2036, with capable line robots following around 2039; those are different moments for our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the records change and 71 when robots could climb. If our savings and pension grew, I might stop before the second date, but neither is guaranteed today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d check my pension projection every year and continue the line job while my body allows it. In 2037 I’d take paid equipment testing shifts if they existed, and Leena and I would decide whether to retire by comparing projected income with bills; if we needed wages, I’d apply for a maintenance post rather than wait until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a bit lighter imagining ten years. I still want a plan that works if my shoulder gives out before a robot ever touches a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you teach anything before retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show younger crew members how I check motor drives, but only when the company gives us paid time to do it. I am not an expert in every kind of line equipment yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leena plan at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena wants us to travel after work ends, and I want that too. We would first work out whether rent and health costs fit the pension statement; the holiday can wait for a real number.

say: I’d ask for **training and retirement choices** during the decade before robots reach lines.
I’d explain **2036 records** come before capable line robots around 2039.
think: I might retire before **71**, but savings and pension growth are uncertain.
A **shoulder problem** could end climbing sooner than technology does.
do: Check my **pension projection** yearly and keep safe line shifts.
Take **paid equipment testing** in 2037 if offered.
Apply for **maintenance work** if retirement income still falls short.
feel: I feel **lighter but practical** about health, pay and the actual pension numbers.
S4.quote: I still want a plan that works if my shoulder gives out before a robot ever touches a wire.
fieldNote: Ivan uses the longer runway for **yearly pension checks** and conditional paid equipment testing.
He wants retirement travel with Leena, but treats **rent and health costs** as the deciding figures.

steps.text: Check the pension projection yearly against rent and health costs
Keep safe line shifts and take paid equipment testing if offered
Apply for maintenance work if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I would be 63 when robots reached line repairs, and I cannot assume our five months of savings would carry us to retirement. A funded course tied to an advertised maintenance opening would help, as would union access to the company’s actual staffing plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when an AI answer is wrong. I caught a bad clearance in my practice quiz yesterday, but the manual would not pop up by itself on a busy pole. The worker must still know enough to doubt the screen.

headlineQuote: The worker must still know enough to doubt the screen.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate and earlier experience maintaining building lifts.
He and partner Leena have about **five months of expenses** saved, while her clinic job supplies another income.
He uses **AI daily** for line study, checks every answer against the manual and enjoys testing new equipment.
Across scenarios, he seeks **funded maintenance training** and real vacancies while testing retirement against a written projection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Ivan most because capable robots could reach his line job before he can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course** tied to an advertised maintenance post and access to staffing plans would give him a real option.
